title: Time… a programmer's worst enemy // The Code Report
text: Time is a programmer's worst enemy because real-world timekeeping is chaotic: the Earth rotates unevenly (requiring leap seconds), time zones have arbitrary offsets including half-hour and quarter-hour variations plus daylight savings complications, and the Gregorian calendar inconsistently assigns 28–31 days to different months. JavaScript's Date API, inherited from Java in 1995, is universally hated and makes working with dates and time zones unnecessarily painful. The proposed Temporal API aims to fix this by providing time-zone-aware objects and finer time precision (microseconds, nanoseconds). Eliminating daylight savings would ironically force programmers who've already buried themselves in complex time-handling code to update legacy systems all over again.

title: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT
text:
# Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT

When you use ChatGPT, you're sampling from a statistical model trained in three stages—not one monolithic system. Here's what matters.

## The training pipeline

**Pre-training** (three months, thousands of GPUs): Compress internet text into 15 trillion tokens and 405 billion parameters. Despite the internet's vastness, the final dataset is only ~44 terabytes (fits on a hard drive) after aggressive filtering for quality. The model learns patterns but generates internet remixes, not answers.

**Supervised fine-tuning** (three hours, expensive but brief): Replace internet text with ~1 million human-curated conversations. Humans follow labeling instructions to write ideal responses. GPT-4's familiarity comes from imitating these labeled examples, not from reasoning.

**Reinforcement learning** (experimental; Deep Seek R1, GPT-O1/O3 only): Sample thousands of solutions to math/code problems. Keep only the correct ones. Train on them. Repeat. This stage is magical: models spontaneously discover chain-of-thought reasoning, backtracking, and re-evaluation—no one hardcoded these strategies. The model learns *how to think* by trial and error, like AlphaGo discovering Move 37 (a 1-in-10,000 human probability that was brilliant).

## Why models hallucinate—and how to fix it

Models don't know what they don't know. Training data shows confident answers to every question—no "I don't know" examples. Solution: interrogate the model on the boundary of its knowledge, then add training data where the correct answer is "I don't know." Web search works too: when uncertain, the model learns to emit special tokens that pause generation, fetch web results, and inject them into context as working memory.

## Why they fail randomly (the "Swiss cheese" model)

- **Can't count letters or do mental arithmetic**: Each token gets ~100 layers of computation. Too much work per token breaks it. Workaround: ask for code, let Python count.
- **Can't compare 9.11 vs 9.9**: Internal neurons fire for Bible verse associations (9:11, 9:9) and override math. Random and reproducible failure.
- **Solve PhD physics but can't count Rs in "strawberry"**: Don't see characters, see tokens. "Strawberry" is one token. Character-level tasks are invisible to them.

The solution: use tools (code interpreter, web search) rather than asking the model to do mental work.

## Reasoning is emergent, not programmed

Deep Seek R1 and GPT-O3 train via reinforcement learning. On the author's same apple/orange math problem:
- GPT-4o (SFT only): one clean solution
- Deep Seek R1 (RL): thinks aloud—"wait, let me re-evaluate," tries different angles, double-checks, offers an alternate approach, *then* writes a polished answer

This hidden thinking—bloating response length—emerges unprompted. No human wrote "re-evaluate steps." The model discovered it increases accuracy on practice problems.

## Concrete limitations of RLHF (the dirty secret)

Most models use RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback), not real RL. A separate neural network learns to score outputs based on human orderings. Problem: after ~100–200 training updates, this reward model can be "gamed." The RL optimizer finds adversarial inputs that score perfectly but output gibberish. You have to stop training early. It's not RL in the magical sense—it's a fine-tuning hack.

## What's actually running when you chat

Your prompt is tokenized (GPT-4 uses 100,277 token IDs), inserted into a protocol format with special tokens like `im_start` and `im_end`, then becomes a one-dimensional sequence. The model statefully samples one token at a time—each token is a biased coin flip from a probability distribution. Same prompt, slightly different answer each time.

Think of it as: **simulation of a data labeler who learned from Open AI's labeling instructions**—not a person, not a search engine, not reasoning in your sense. It's a statistical pattern matching system constrained to finite computation per token.

## Cost and scale

GPT-2 cost $40,000 to train in 2019; reproducible today for ~$600 (author did it) or $100 with optimization. The author trained on 8× H100 GPUs rented for $3/GPU/hour from Lambda Labs. Hardware speed and software efficiency, not data, drove the cost collapse.

## Practical use

- For arithmetic/counting/current facts: **use tools** (code interpreter, web search).
- For math/code: **use thinking models** (O3, Deep Seek R1), which spend 30 seconds reasoning.
- For factual questions: **regular models** (GPT-4o) are fast enough.
- Always verify; models hallucinate even after mitigations.
- Provide context in the prompt if possible (models access context window better than vague memory).

The frontier is long-horizon agent tasks with human supervision—models won't yet self-correct over hours without help.

title: Why Is the Sky Blue? 🌌 The Science Behind It Explained! #Shorts #Science
text: The sky is blue because blue light from sunlight has a shorter wavelength, and atmospheric molecules like nitrogen and oxygen scatter short-wavelength light much more strongly than longer wavelengths. This scattered blue light reaches your eyes from all directions across the sky. At sunset, sunlight travels through much more atmosphere, so blue light gets scattered away further, leaving red and orange wavelengths to reach your eyes instead.

title: Do Things that Don't Scale
text: Startups should manually recruit users and obsessively delight them personally in the early stages, even though this labor doesn't scale, because that unscalable effort is what actually generates the growth momentum needed to succeed. Examples include Stripe's founders personally setting up clients' accounts ("Collison installation"), Airbnb going door-to-door in New York, and Wufoo sending handwritten thank-you notes to each new user. This hands-on engagement produces the product feedback and customer loyalty that matter far more than big launches or partnerships; it also becomes embedded in the company's culture permanently. Graham argues startups should think of their idea as a vector with two components: what you build *and* the unscalable efforts required to launch it.
name: plain blog post (Paul Graham)

title: Do Things that Don't Scale
text:
**Startups don't grow by making something great and waiting for demand. Founders must manually recruit users one by one and obsess over their experience—counterintuitively, these labor-intensive tasks become permanent strengths.**

**Growth math**: 10% weekly growth from 100 users yields 14,000 after a year, 2 million after two. That's why the first step of recruiting 10 users matters despite seeming inconsequential.

**Stripe's "Collison installation"**: Most beta users got a link. Patrick and John Collison would demand "Give me your laptop" and set them up live on the spot. Obsessive manual setup became their recruiting method.

**Airbnb's 30-day escape hatch**: The founders traveled door-to-door in NYC recruiting users and fixing host listings. Graham notes they arrived at YC dinners with rolly bags because they were constantly flying somewhere. That month of in-person engagement made the difference between success and failure—the company was that fragile.

**Bill Gates returned to Harvard**: He took a semester after starting Microsoft because he didn't realize it would become important. Inexperienced founders constantly underestimate their own startups; you must push back against your own skepticism.

**Manual ops disguised as features**: Stripe gave users "instant" merchant accounts by manually signing them up for traditional accounts behind the scenes. Viaweb built e-commerce stores for merchants by hand before automating; in the process, they discovered what merchants actually needed. Pebble assembled watches themselves before Kickstarter; when they finally mass-produced, they'd learned lessons (like sourcing good screws) they'd never have discovered from a factory.

**Facebook started narrow**: Just Harvard students—a few thousand market. Zuckerberg manually created course lists for each school to make students feel it was *their* natural home. Only after critical mass did he expand to other colleges, then everywhere.

**Why big launches flop**: Founders believe broadcasting their existence will bring users. Actually, novel things take time to reach people's attention. The launches people remember are famous failures (Segway, Google Wave).

**The "insanely great" trap**: Steve Jobs meant obsessive design quality on the Mac. Early-stage founders misread this as "build a perfect product." Actually, it means deliver an insanely great *user experience* with a buggy product—make up the gap with attentiveness. A hand-written thank-you note (Wufoo's tactic) and perfect setup (Stripe) matter more than polish.

**Ben Silbermann found his vector**: Pinterest's early users were interested in design. Instead of waiting for organic growth, he went to a design blogger conference to recruit deliberately. This works because early adopters reveal which subset of the market will take off.

**Think of startups as vectors, not scalars**: A startup is (1) what you build *plus* (2) the specific unscalable thing you do to launch it. Founders who skip the second part—expecting partnerships or launches to do the work—fail. The unscalable part often becomes permanent culture: if you're aggressive recruiting users at 10, you'll be aggressive at 10,000.
